transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The investigation into last week's mid-air attack on a Dubai-to-Televis flight finds
the co-pilot who attacked the captain intended to crash the commercial airliner into Israel's
Ben Gurion Airport.
That's according to a person not authorized to speak publicly on the matter, and Pierre's
Kat Lonsdorf has more from Tel Aviv.
A source familiar with the investigation told NPR that the co-pilot who attacked the captain
mid-air intended to fly the plane to Ben Gurion, which was its destination, but then crash
it into the airport.
That source also said it's likely the co-pilot acted alone.
Officials from both the United Arab Emirates and Israel have said that the incident was
an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still unclear.
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials, raising questions about how he was
allowed to fly a plane heading to Israel.
Israel only allows pilots from countries it has diplomatic relations with to enter its
airspace.
Israel said it's opening an examination into how that happened.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Member Station WSKG reports a Cornell University administrative building was vandalized early
this morning, underscoring anger on and off campus over the Ivy League school's handling
of a 2024 case in which a woman says she was gang-raped by members of a fraternity.
The woman, identified as Jane Doe, filed suit weeks ago.
The New York state AG is now overseeing a criminal probe.
Cornell's president denounced the vandalism as he again acknowledged growing criticism
of how the school handled the case under the federal law Title IX.
Civil rights lawyer Alexandra Brodsky has written about sexual harassment at schools.
Title IX over the years has become a much less effective tool for survivors.
The Supreme Court has issued opinions that make it very hard for students to meet the
necessary standards to make out a case in court.
And also the Supreme Court has narrowed the types of damages that a student can get.
Brodsky on NPR's Here and Now.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is throwing its support behind six additional
candidates ahead of the November midterm elections.
NPR's Tamara Keith reports the six candidates are running in districts where Republicans
have an edge.
Kennedy's Red to Blue is its top-tier backing for candidates and comes with staff resources
and fundraising support.
All six candidates newly added to the list face challenging races.
Only one is in a district rated by the Cook Political Report as lean Republican.
The others face even longer odds.
For instance, Nevada's second congressional district where candidate Teresa Benitez-Thompson
earned the Red to Blue nod.
That district has not elected a Democrat since its creation in the early 1980s, a spokesman
for the National Republican Congressional Committee said describing that race as competitive
is delusional.
Tamara Keith, NPR News.
From Washington, this is NPR.
Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert has died at the age of 84.
The former Illinois lawmaker was the longest-serving Republican Speaker of the House but saw his
political legacy tarnished after leaving office when he admitted in court to having sexually
abused teenage boys during his years as a high school wrestling coach.
A new report finds schools across the United States restricted more than 7,000 unique book
titles in some way in the 2025-26 academic school year.
And Pierre-Xandrew Limbong reports on the findings from the free speech organization
PEN America.
According to PEN America, upwards of 7,000 is a "record number of unique titles banned."
The organization defines a ban as any restriction placed on books overriding the recommendations
of educators and librarians.
Some of the most commonly banned titles across school districts include Speak by Lori Hals-Anderson,
The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood, and Kingdom of Ash by Sarah J. Mass.
According to the report, the vast majority of bans come from Texas and Florida.
The report also noted a growing trend of AI being used to evaluate books, where the AI
chatbots will recommend books to be banned not because they meet a legal standard but
because other school districts have banned them.
Andrew Limbong, NPR News.
Several top congressional Democrats are urging the Federal Aviation Administration not to
roll back a requirement that U.S. airlines must keep epinephrine on their flights in
the event of a medical emergency.
And August the FAA proposed giving airlines more discretion in setting medical response
standards.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News.

topics.text: Co-pilot who attacked captain on Dubai flight intended to crash plane into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport
Cornell University administrative building vandalized over school's handling of alleged 2024 fraternity gang rape case
Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee backs six additional candidates in challenging races for November midterm elections
Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert dies at age 84 after conviction for sexually abusing teenage wrestlers
Schools restricted over 7,000 unique book titles in 2025-26 school year, with most bans in Texas and Florida
Congressional Democrats urge FAA not to roll back requirement for U.S. airlines to carry epinephrine on flights
